Experimental grammar: a likelihood comparison study

Source: vignettes/experimental-likelihood-study.Rmd
experimental-likelihood-study.Rmd

How do likelihood, link and predictor choices affect prediction and coefficient recovery? The choice-of-likelihood study compares these choices on positive and unit-interval responses. This vignette expresses its configured designs with an experimental study grammar. Knitting builds plans and exercises a comparison on invented scores; it fits no models.

The design tables follow the study’s pinned source. The executable generator and brms adapter below cover a smaller, explicitly defined example. They are not an exact reproduction of the historical simulations. The source scripts rely on historical helpers and custom families that this example does not restore. These declarations are separate from the supported simulation_config() engine.

The helper file is installed with the package and contains ordinary R functions:

system.file("experimental", "likelihood-case.R", package = "bayesim")
#> [1] "/home/runner/work/_temp/Library/bayesim/experimental/likelihood-case.R"

Conditions and candidates

The full positive-response design contains eight generating families, three response shapes, and null or nonzero effects. Its filters constrain the allowed links. The unit-interval design contains six generating families and its own shape-specific coefficient tables. Each candidate combines a fitting family, a link and one of five predictor formulas. The helper retains all source coefficient and dispersion values, including the altered structural coefficients for the unit-interval bathtub shape. Positive source, unit-interval source.

positive <- likelihood_design("positive")
unit <- likelihood_design("unit")
stopifnot(
  nrow(positive$conditions) == 84L, nrow(positive$candidates) == 85L,
  nrow(unit$conditions) == 72L, nrow(unit$candidates) == 80L
)
positive$conditions[1:3, c("condition_id", "data_N", "dataset_N",
                          "x_y_coef", "sigma_y", "y_intercept")]
#>                       condition_id data_N dataset_N x_y_coef sigma_y
#> 1   positive:gamma:log:ramp:effect    100       200     0.25       1
#> 2 positive:weibull:log:ramp:effect    100       200     0.25       1
#> 5 positive:frechet:log:ramp:effect    100       200     0.25       2
#>   y_intercept
#> 1           0
#> 2           0
#> 5           0
unique(positive$candidates$formula)
#> [1] "y ~ x + z1 + z2"      "y ~ x + z2"           "y ~ x + z1"          
#> [4] "y ~ x + z1 + z2 + z3" "y ~ x + z1 + z2 + z4"

data_N = 100 specifies observations; dataset_N = 200 specifies dataset replicates. The historical runner generated one dataset before looping over candidate fits. The experimental grammar also puts methods under a shared dataset identity. The cited historical commit establishes that structure; it does not establish which version produced the study’s saved results.

The source leaves some link helpers implicit. Here the inverse-softplus link is log(expm1(mu)), logit is qlogis(mu), cauchit is qcauchy(mu), and complementary log-log is log(-log1p(-mu)). These are explicit interpretations used to resolve the coefficient tables, not verified copies of those helpers.

Literal links and coefficient meaning

A lognormal candidate has literal link identity in the source, but its coefficient acts on a logarithmic scale. The postprocessing records effective links separately. Both fields belong in the declaration:

unique(positive$candidates[c("fit_family", "fit_link", "effective_link")])
#>          fit_family fit_link effective_link
#> 1  inverse.gaussian      log            log
#> 2          gompertz      log            log
#> 3             gamma      log            log
#> 4           weibull      log            log
#> 7           frechet      log            log
#> 8         betaprime      log            log
#> 9          gaussian      log            log
#> 10 inverse.gaussian softplus       softplus
#> 11         gompertz softplus       softplus
#> 12            gamma softplus       softplus
#> 13          weibull softplus       softplus
#> 16          frechet softplus       softplus
#> 17        betaprime softplus       softplus
#> 18         gaussian softplus       softplus
#> 23        lognormal identity            log
#> 24   softplusnormal identity       softplus
#> 27         gaussian identity       identity

For the illustrative generator, recovery of the generating x coefficient is reported only when the candidate’s effective link matches the generating link. Here comparable means that the coefficient is evaluated on the chosen link scale, not that the candidate identifies the generating effect. The formulas that omit z1 or condition on the post-outcome variable z4 are deliberately misspecified. Their errors against x_y_coef remain in the recovery analysis to show the consequences of those choices. Restricting analysis to correctly adjusted formulas would answer a different question. Matching names or links alone does not establish coefficient comparability for another study. Predictive scores can still enter a comparison when recovery is unavailable.

Scientific functions and artifact needs

likelihood_generate_subset(condition, context) implements an illustrative structural model. It generates independent normal z1, z2 and z3, then sets x from z1, z3 and normal noise. Its response predictor is y_intercept + x_y_coef*x + z1_y_coef*z1 + z2_y_coef*z2. Gamma/log conditions use mean exp(eta) and shape sigma_y; Beta/logit conditions use mean plogis(eta) and precision sigma_y. Finally, z4 depends on x, y and normal noise. Training and testing data use separate draws of this model.

This generator supports Gamma/log and Beta/logit only. It omits the source’s response-bound rejection/resampling settings. It stops on other conditions. The full grids therefore document planning coverage; the subset below identifies execution coverage. A replacement generator must state its own parameterization and handling of response bounds.

likelihood_fit(data, context) calls brms::brm() using the method’s formula, family, link and seed. It uses CmdStan, four chains and 2,000 iterations. These are example settings, not recovered historical settings. It requires brms and CmdStan when executed; unsupported custom families report an error. Namespace calls sit inside functions, so planning loads neither backend nor models.

The extractors produce chain-preserving slope draws, sampler diagnostics and pointwise LOO scores. likelihood_measure() computes bias, posterior root mean squared error against truth, sign probability, interval exclusion of zero and summed LOO ELPD. The posterior error quantity is explicitly sqrt(mean((draws - truth)^2)); its rmse_s name supports the example policy but does not certify equivalence to an unavailable historical metric helper. These choices are ordinary functions, rather than inferred metric names.

positive_study <- likelihood_declaration(positive, "positive-likelihoods")
unit_study <- likelihood_declaration(unit, "unit-likelihoods")

positive_plan <- plan_study(positive_study, replicates = 200L, seed = 1235813L)
unit_plan <- plan_study(unit_study, replicates = 200L, seed = 1235813L)

configured_counts <- data.frame(
  domain = c("positive", "unit interval"),
  conditions = c(nrow(positive$conditions), nrow(unit$conditions)),
  replicates = 200L,
  candidates = c(nrow(positive$candidates), nrow(unit$candidates))
)
configured_counts$fits <- with(configured_counts, conditions * replicates * candidates)
configured_counts
#>          domain conditions replicates candidates    fits
#> 1      positive         84        200         85 1428000
#> 2 unit interval         72        200         80 1152000

These are configured combinations, not observed completed fits or promises that all historical family/link combinations are supported. The counts include Gaussian with every listed link because that is what the source filters allow. plan_study() validates declarations and artifact dependencies. It does not call the generator, validate a backend family, prepare a model or sample a prior.

A smaller declaration has a fully specified generator and built-in candidate families. It keeps all five source formulas and both null and nonzero effects:

gamma_example <- list(
  conditions = subset(positive$conditions, data_family == "gamma" & data_link == "log"),
  candidates = subset(positive$candidates, fit_family == "gamma" & fit_link == "log")
)
beta_example <- list(
  conditions = subset(unit$conditions, data_family == "beta" & data_link == "logit"),
  candidates = subset(unit$candidates, fit_family == "beta" & fit_link == "logit")
)
gamma_study <- likelihood_declaration(gamma_example, "illustrative-gamma")
beta_study <- likelihood_declaration(beta_example, "illustrative-beta")
gamma_plan <- plan_study(gamma_study, replicates = 2L, seed = 42L)
beta_plan <- plan_study(beta_study, replicates = 2L, seed = 42L)
stopifnot(nrow(gamma_example$conditions) == 6L,
          nrow(beta_example$conditions) == 6L,
          nrow(gamma_example$candidates) == 5L,
          nrow(beta_example$candidates) == 5L)

A comparison is a grouped calculation

The declaration uses by = c("dataset_id", "method_formula"). Within each group, likelihood_elpd_gap() subtracts the best finite ELPD from each score. It returns the size of the reference set alongside each gap. This is a measurement-row comparison; it needs no retained native fit.

The source filters diagnostics, missing values and extreme errors before computing its maxima. Changing that policy can change the reference model. This cheap example uses invented scores, where the best predictor has an unacceptable R-hat:

example_rows <- data.frame(
  method_id = c("A", "B", "C"), measurement = "performance",
  value = c(0.1, 0.2, 0.3), rmse_s = 0.5, comparable = TRUE,
  elpd_loo = c(-102, -100, -99), rhat = c(1, 1, 1.1),
  ess_bulk = 800, ess_tail = 800, divergents = 0
)
raw_gaps <- likelihood_elpd_gap(example_rows, list(), list())
selected <- example_rows[likelihood_selection(example_rows, data.frame()), , drop = FALSE]
selected_gaps <- likelihood_elpd_gap(selected, list(), list())
raw_gaps
#>   candidate value n_reference
#> 1         A    -3           3
#> 2         B    -1           3
#> 3         C     0           3
selected_gaps
#>   candidate value n_reference
#> 1         A    -2           2
#> 2         B     0           2
stopifnot(identical(raw_gaps$value, c(-3, -1, 0)),
          identical(selected_gaps$value, c(-2, 0)))

likelihood_selection(measurements, attempts) states a recovery-analysis policy: comparable coefficients, finite scores and recovery measures, at most 10 divergences, R-hat at most 1.01, both ESS measures above 400, absolute bias below 10 and posterior error below 10. This example does not reproduce every historical filter: it omits predictive RMSE, new-data ELPD and later Pareto-k filters. Keep those choices explicit when extending it.

After an authorized run, assess_study(run, policy = likelihood_selection) keeps raw rows and exclusions, then reruns this comparison on selected rows. Failed attempts remain in the run’s attempt records. Downstream brms, lmer or custom plotting code can use the resulting tables and dataset identities. No downstream analysis is needed to construct these plans.
